accepted.question_text: Consider the single-channel slotted multiple-access problem with n indistinguishable users, where after each slot every user receives perfect feedback giving the exact number of transmitters F[t] on that slot, and the objective is to minimize the expected time until the first successful transmission. The paper develops an efficiently computable policy for arbitrary positive integers n: users randomize on the first slot, use the observed collision size to partition themselves into groups, and then recursively continue with the more favorable subgroup. Is this policy optimal for every positive integer n, or can some other decentralized policy achieve a smaller expected time to first success for some values of n?
accepted.context_brief: Optimality of the n-user capture policy

evidence.quote: This identifies two open questions that we leave to future work: (i) Is the algorithm of this paper optimal for all values of n?
It is not clear if gains can be achieved by keeping track of an ever-increasing number of groups and having multiple groups probabilistically transmit at the same time.
Clearly 1 <= z_n^* <= z_n, where z_n are the values associated with the proposed algorithm of the previous section. The author conjectures that z_n = z_n^* for all n.
An efficient policy was developed for any positive integer n. Whether or not this policy is optimal for all n is left as an open question.

accepted.question_text: In the same decentralized channel-capture setting, the paper assumes that after every slot each user is told the exact number of users who transmitted, so that F[t]=0 means idle, F[t]=1 means success, and F[t]>=2 means a collision with a known number of transmitters. If that exact transmitter-count feedback is not available and users instead receive more limited feedback, what decentralized algorithms are then optimal for minimizing the expected time to the first success or otherwise achieving optimal channel-capture performance?

evidence.quote: This identifies two open questions that we leave to future work: (ii) What algorithms are optimal when more limited feedback information is used?
If n = 2 then F[t] is equivalent to the idle, success, collision feedback of classical slotted Aloha. If n > 2 then the F[t] feedback is more detailed.

accepted.question_text: Extend the model to n users and m orthogonal channels, where on each slot a user may choose any subset of channels on which to transmit and the receiver reports the per-channel transmitter counts. Is it optimal to run the single-channel capture policy separately and independently on each channel, or can coupling a user's transmission decisions across channels produce strictly better expected time to the first success? More generally, for which combinations of user count and channel count is per-channel independence optimal, and when is cross-channel correlation necessary for optimality?
accepted.context_brief: Optimality of independent versus correlated multi-channel policies

evidence.quote: One way to extend the transmission schemes of this paper to a multi-channel environment is to implement them separately and independently over each channel. Is such separate and independent implementation optimal, or can correlating the transmission decisions over each channel provide efficiency gains?
The goal is to minimize E [Z]. Is it optimal to use all channels separately and independently? The answer is different when n = 2 versus n = 3.

It was shown that, for the context of minimizing the expected time to first capture, it is optimal to independently use all channels when the number of users is only two. However, a counter-example was shown for the case of three users and two channels: Optimality requires each user to correlate its transmission decisions over each channel, rather than independently use each channel.
